classification.summary: Discusses principles, ethical issues, and clinical practice surrounding placebo use in medicine as a dialogue on trust, deception, and physician–patient relations.

title: Can placebo therapy influence arterial blood pressure?
abstract: 1. With standard sphygmomanometric techniques used in conjunction with continuous intra-arterial monitoring the antihypertensive effect of placebo was examined in a group of patients participating in a controlled clinical trial. 2. Twelve of the 20 patients entered completed all stages of a randomized double-blind controlled trial of placebo and indoramin. Clinic blood pressure in patients receiving placebo showed reductions which were highly significant (P less than 0.001). Simultaneous intra-arterial monitoring showed no reduction of the blood pressure over the 24 h studied. 3. The clinic pressures showed minimal reduction of blood pressure in response to indoramin therapy whereas intra-arterial pressures showed a significant fall (P less than 0.01). 4. The response of the blood pressure to placebo appears to be an artifact of the indirect sphygmomanometric method and its use as a control in this study led to under-estimation of the efficacy of indoramin.

screening.rationale: Randomized trial explicitly examined placebo's antihypertensive effect and compared placebo-arm clinic reductions with invasive intra-arterial measurements, making placebo response the study focus.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial examined placebo's antihypertensive effect and found large clinic sphygmomanometer reductions on placebo but no concurrent intra-arterial blood pressure fall, suggesting a measurement artifact.
classification.key_finding: Placebo produced significant clinic blood pressure reductions (p<0.001) but no change in continuous intra-arterial BP, indicating peripheral measurement artifact and underestimation of active drug efficacy.

title: Cognitive activity and suggestions for analgesia in the reduction of reported pain.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and title alone is insufficient to confirm that placebo/nocebo phenomena were the explicit focus or whether experimental contrasts isolating placebo effects were used.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated an empirical study of cognitive activity and suggestions (hypnosis) for analgesia in humans, but methods and focus on placebo/nocebo effects were unclear.

title: Effects of cue-controlled relaxation, a credible placebo treatment and no treatment on shyness among college males.
journal: Journal of behavior therapy and experimental psychiatry

screening.rationale: Title indicates an experiment contrasting a credible placebo treatment against no treatment to affect shyness, meeting the placebo-effect design criterion (placebo vs no treatment).

classification.summary: Compared cue-controlled relaxation, a credible placebo treatment, and no treatment on shyness in college males; abstract/results were not available.

title: The effect of explicit expectations on initial meditation experiences.
abstract: Although meditation has been employed successfully as a treatment for various stress-related disorders, there is still little evidence clarifying just which aspects of meditation training are responsible for these therapeutic effects. This experiment sought to test the hypothesis that creating two opposite expectations about an initial meditation experience would result in differing physiological and phenomenological responses, even though the same technique was practiced by all subjects. The results of the experiment failed to support this hypothesis.

screening.rationale: Randomized manipulation of explicit expectations about the same meditation technique tested whether context/expectation changed physiological and phenomenological responses, meeting criterion for an experimental placebo/context effect.

classification.summary: Randomized study manipulated opposite expectations about an initial meditation experience and found no reliable differences in physiological or phenomenological responses between groups.
classification.key_finding: Explicit expectation manipulation did not alter self-reported experience or autonomic measures during initial meditation.

title: Anxiety and placebo reaction in neurotic patients.
journal: Agressologie: revue internationale de physio-biologie et de pharmacologie appliquees aux effets de l'agression

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses 'placebo reaction' in neurotic (anxiety/phobic) patients, indicating placebo response was the study focus despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Studied placebo reactions in neurotic (anxiety/phobic) patients and reported on placebo response characteristics in that clinical sample.

title: Placebo-psychotherapy combinations: inappropriate representations of psychotherapy in drug-psychotherapy comparative trials.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper critiques placebo-psychotherapy representations in drug–psychotherapy trials, making placebo methodology the paper's main subject (a review/commentary).

classification.summary: Reviewed and critiqued how psychotherapy was represented and how placebos were used in drug–psychotherapy comparative trials, arguing these representations were inappropriate.

title: A further study of described context effect and noise annoyance ratings.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available to determine whether the study explicitly investigated placebo/nocebo (context) effects on annoyance versus merely measuring context as an attitude correlate.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggested an investigation of context effects on noise annoyance but methods and whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were the focus were unclear.

title: Morphine tolerance in rats: congruence with a Pavlovian paradigm.
journal: Journal of comparative and physiological psychology
abstract: Evidence for associational and nonassociational mechanisms of tolerance development was found in four experiments using an automated flinch/jump assessment of morphine's analgesic effects. Rats receiving morphine in a distinctive environment displayed greater tolerance when tested in that environment than animals receiving equal but unpaired exposure to the drug and environment. This context effect occurred at low (5 mg/kg) and moderate (20 mg/kg) doses and was attenuated by predrug exposure to the tolerance-test environment. This attenuation was found to be due to latent inhibition rather than to stress induction or novelty reduction. In general, results of this series of experiments support a Pavlovian model of contextually mediated tolerance and are inconsistent with other explanations.

screening.rationale: Animal experiments tested Pavlovian/contextual modulation of morphine analgesic tolerance (contextual conditioning of drug effect), matching inclusion rule for conditioning mechanisms in nonhuman models.

classification.summary: Found that rats developed greater morphine tolerance when drug administration was paired with a distinctive context, supporting a Pavlovian/contextual model of tolerance.
classification.key_finding: Contextual pairing of morphine produced reliable conditioned tolerance (reduced analgesic flinch/jump response) compared with unpaired exposure; latent inhibition of the context attenuated the effect.

title: An expectancy-attribution model of the effects of placebos.

screening.rationale: Theory paper that explicitly proposes a psychological expectancy-attribution model of placebo effects, making placebo the primary subject (fits Rule 4/5).

classification.summary: Proposed an expectancy-attribution theoretical model explaining how expectancies and attributions produce placebo effects and shape responses to inert treatments.

title: Actions of salbutamol, disodium cromoglycate, and placebo administered as aerosols in acute asthma.
abstract: The effects on the peak expiratory flow rate of the drug sequences, placebo-salbutamol-disodium cromoglycate and placebo-disodium cromoglycate-salbutamol administered via a nebuliser were examined in 35 children with asthma. Twenty children were each examined once within 4 hours of admission to hospital with an acute attack of asthma, and the remaining 15 children were examined later in the attack on two occasions. The placebo effect of sterile water accounted for about half of the total bronchodilator action both early and late in the attack. It is suggested that this effect is due to the action of water on the surface film of surfactant, causing collapse of bubbles and strands or webs of mucoid material, thus decreasing airways resistance. At this time salbutamol is significantly more potent than disodium cromoglycate as a bronchodilator agent.

screening.rationale: Clinical trial explicitly quantified the placebo (sterile water) effect on peak expiratory flow, making placebo response an analytic focus.

classification.summary: Found that sterile water aerosol (placebo) produced about half of the bronchodilator increase in peak expiratory flow in 35 children with acute asthma.
classification.key_finding: Placebo (sterile water) accounted for ~50% of the bronchodilator action on peak expiratory flow.

title: Variability of exercise performance during long-term placebo treatment.
abstract: Although exercise testing is commonly used to determine the efficacy of antianginal drugs, there is little information on the effect of frequent exposure to such testing over periods of long as 6 mo. In or study 10 patients (four men and six women) with stable angina pectoris received placebo for 6 mo. Treadmill testing followed a modified Bruce protocol. All patients exercised to an end point of typical anginal pain and 1 mm or more of ST depression. The first treadmill test for diagnostic purposes was followed by testing every 2 wk for 6 mo. Sublingual nitroglycerin was permitted to abort attacks of angina. Parameters evaluated included heart rate, double product, and duration of exercise. There was no change in the maximal heart rate (mean = 109 at 2 wk and 112 at 6 mo) or double product (mean = 17,002 at 2 wk and 17,249 at 6 mo). On the other hand, duration increased (mean 7.8 min at two wk and 9.9 min at 6 mo). Thus, although treadmill testing showed reproducible measurements of maximal heart rate and double product over 6 mo, exercise duration increased progressively.

screening.rationale: Placebo-treated arm over 6 months was the analytic focus, assessing placebo-associated changes in exercise performance (placebo response).

classification.summary: Studied 10 angina patients given placebo for 6 months and found exercise duration increased over time while maximal heart rate and double product did not change.
classification.key_finding: Found progressive increase in treadmill exercise duration (mean 7.8 to 9.9 min) over 6 months on placebo despite stable heart-rate and double-product measures.

title: A survey of placebo use in a general hospital.
abstract: Two hundred thirty registered nurses and seventy physicians participated in a retrospective study scrutinizing placebo effects, prescribing patterns, and staff attitudes in a university-based general hospital setting. Despite copious experimental literature devoted to placebo effects over the past thirty years, the medical and surgical use of placebos seems to disregard experimental data. Although 80% of the staff had used placebos in the hospital, their knowledge of placebo effects was in many respects deficient. Within the hospital, 89% of placebo use was directed toward the amelioration of "pain"; the authors believe that emphasis should be placed on the education of staff to perceive emotional, social, and physiological concomitants of pain rather than resorting to a purely physicalistic approach. A need to acknowledge staff conflicts over the ethical use of placebos should be a significant part of this educational approach.

screening.rationale: Survey of hospital staff attitudes and prescribing of placebos directly studies placebo use and ethics (placebo science/clinical use topic).

classification.summary: Surveyed 230 nurses and 70 physicians about hospital placebo prescribing, finding widespread use and gaps in knowledge and ethical concerns, with most uses directed at pain.
classification.key_finding: Found 80% of staff reported using placebos and 89% of placebo use was aimed at ameliorating pain.

title: Managing for placebo effects.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and the title suggests a managerial/commentary piece about placebo effects, so available information is insufficient to determine whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were an empirical focus.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to judge; no abstract was available and the title suggests a commentary on managing placebo effects in hospitals.

title: Selective monitoring of physical sensations.
journal: Journal of personality and social psychology
abstract: Two experiments demonstrated that the experience of physical sensations is the result of hypothesis-guided selective search and encoding. In the first experiment, subjects listened to a stimulus that was said to increase, decrease, or have no effect on skin temperature. The results indicated that subjects selectively monitored only those changes in skin temperature congruent with the experimentally induced hypotheses, thus resulting in self-reports of change in skin temperature in the suggested directions. Two replications using heart rate and nasal congestion-which imposed search strategies-produced comparable results. In Experiment 2, subjects viewed a heartbeat chart and assessed the degree to which a hypothetical drug influenced a target person's heart rate. Perceptions of change in heart rate were influenced by both experimentally induced hypotheses as well as subjects' perceptions of their own heart rate. That is, if prior to the experiment subjects believed their own pulse was accelerated, they were more likely to perceive the graphed heartbeat accelerating as well. The findings point to parallels between perception of internal state and the external environment. Finally, the roles of hypothesis-guided selective search are extended to placebo effectiveness.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of hypotheses/expectations produced selective self-reported bodily changes, so placebo-related expectation mechanisms were the study's focus (experimental suggestion effects on perceived physiology).

classification.summary: Found that experimentally induced hypotheses about bodily changes biased selective monitoring and self-reports of skin temperature, heart rate, and nasal congestion, linking expectation-driven perception to placebo effectiveness.
classification.key_finding: Verbal suggestion produced congruent self-reported changes in physiological sensations without corresponding objective changes.

title: Biofeedback as a placebo: anxiety reduction facilitated by training in either suppression or enhancement of alpha brainwaves.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title indicates the study tested biofeedback as a placebo with anxiety reduction as the outcome, making placebo phenomena the explicit focus despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Tested biofeedback (alpha enhancement or suppression) as a placebo-style intervention and found anxiety symptoms were reduced following training.
classification.key_finding: Found that alpha biofeedback training produced reductions in self-reported anxiety.

title: Psyllium therapy in the irritable bowel syndrome. A double-blind trial.
abstract: A randomized, double-blind trial of a psyllium preparation was initiated in 77 patients with painful irritable bowel syndrome. Sixty-patients finished and submitted symptom data for 8 weeks while taking placebo (n = 34) or psyllium (n = 26). Increase in normal stools and decrease in pain severity (p less than 0.05) occurred equally in both groups. Subjective improvement was reported by 24 of 34 patients on placebo and 20 or 26 on psyllium (p greater than 0.05). Five symptom variables were significantly correlated (p less than 0.05) with patient's subjective global assessment (R = 0.64). Discriminant analysis of Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory variables yielded overall rates of correct prediction of 66.1% for whether patients got "much better" and 77.9% for whether they voluntarily dropped from the study. A major placebo effect occurs in patients with painful irritable bowel syndrome and is probably responsible for the efficacy of psyllium. Personality factors influence the magnitude of therapeutic response and whether patients discontinue treatment within 8 weeks.

screening.rationale: Although a drug-versus-placebo RCT, the paper analyzed and reported a major placebo response and personality predictors of who improved or dropped out, making placebo response itself an analytic focus.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial in IBS patients found similar improvements in stool frequency and pain in placebo and psyllium groups and identified personality measures that predicted subjective improvement and dropout.
classification.key_finding: Found large subjective improvement in the placebo arm (24/34 reported improvement) and MMPI profiles predicted therapeutic response and discontinuation.

title: Enuresis, homoeopathy, and enhancement of the placebo effect.
journal: The American journal of clinical hypnosis

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses enhancement of the placebo effect in case reports of homeopathy for enuresis, indicating placebo is the paper's subject despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Reported case reports of homeopathic treatment for enuresis and discussed approaches to enhance the placebo effect.

title: The effects of an expectancy state on the fate of applications and psychotherapy in an outpatient setting.
abstract: This study describes an attempt to influence the outcome of outpatient psychotherapy by offering pretherapy information to application. The sample consisted of more than 1,300 applicants; the pretherapy information, in the form of a printed leaflet, was included with the application blank for alternate cases. The results suggest that the pretherapy information tended to discourage the completing of application blanks. Among those patients who eventually participated in psychotherapy, pretherapy information had no effect on the duration of treatment or on treatment outcomes as rated by the therapists. Incidentally, the data indicate that having health insurance has a strong, positive effect on the number of treatment interviews.
mesh: Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated pretherapy information (expectancy) versus no information and measured effects on application completion and psychotherapy outcomes, making expectation/context the focus.

classification.summary: Tested whether a pretherapy informational leaflet altered psychotherapy application rates and outcomes; the leaflet reduced completed applications but did not affect treatment duration or therapist-rated outcomes.
classification.key_finding: Pretherapy information decreased application completion rates but had no effect on psychotherapy duration or therapist-rated outcomes.

title: Comparative credibility of treatment rationales: three tests of expectancy theory.
journal: The British journal of clinical psychology
abstract: Previous research has challenged the adequacy of conventional "placebo' controls, by demonstrating that active treatments, such as systematic desensitization, are more credible than supposedly inert control conditions. Such findings give support to the hypothesis that the arousal of positive expectancies is the key to therapeutic change. Three experiments are reported, in which Borkovec's credibility rating method was applied to treatment comparisons modelled upon the findings of outcome research. In the first experiment, systematic desensitization was more credible than rational-emotive and client-centered therapy (P less than 0.001), consistent with an expectancy-arousal explanation of Di Loreto's (1971) comparative outcome study. In the second experiment, Paul's (1966) attention placebo condition was less credible than three active treatments (P less than 0.001). In the third experiment, in vivo desensitization was in some respects more credible than imaginal desensitization, which was in turn more credible in some respects than relaxation alone (P less than 0.001). The results of the latter two experiments were broadly consistent with an expectancy-arousal interpretation of much outcome literature. These results emphasize the insufficiency of merely including a designated "placebo control condition' in outcome research (Kazdin & Wilcoxon, 1976). Credibility differences did not mirror precisely the results of the outcome research on which these studies were modelled, however. Methodological limitations are discussed, and further clinical research is advocated, in which the persuasiveness of treatment rationales is studied in its own right as contribution to treatment efficacy.
mesh: Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care

screening.rationale: Empirical study focused on treatment credibility/expectancy (placebo-related mechanism) rather than testing an active treatment versus placebo, so fits placebo science (attitudes/expectancy) inclusion.

classification.summary: Compared credibility ratings of treatment rationales across three experiments and found systematic differences supporting expectancy/credibility effects as relevant to psychotherapy outcomes.
classification.key_finding: Found that active therapies and in vivo desensitization produced higher credibility ratings than attention-placebo or relaxation, consistent with an expectancy-arousal account.

title: Placebo-controlled tests of chemical food additives: are they valid?
abstract: Placebo-controlled studies of effects of monosodium L-glutamate (MSG) and mixed synthetic food dyes in humans which have led to claims that these additives are safe in general use may be questioned on 3 methodological grounds: both active substance and placebo may be inadequately specified in published reports and potent common food allergens are used as placebos.

screening.rationale: Paper critiqued the methodology of placebo-controlled studies of food additives and discussed placebo specification and choice of placebo, making placebo science the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Argued that placebo-controlled studies of MSG and synthetic food dyes had methodological flaws, including inadequate specification of active and placebo substances and use of common allergens as placebos.
classification.key_finding: Contended that many placebo-controlled tests of food additives were invalid because placebos were poorly specified and sometimes contained common allergens.

title: Analgesic responses to morphine and placebo in individuals with postoperative pain.
abstract: The effects of placebo and varying doses of intravenous morphine were studied in 74 patients. All patients underwent extraction of impacted mandibular third molars. Two hours after onset of anesthesia all patients received a placebo (intravenous saline). One hour after the placebo administration each patient received either a second placebo or, 4, 6, 8 or 12 mg of morphine, double blind, via a hidden intravenous line. Pain level was evaluated 50 min after morphine administration using a visual analog scale. Pooled data from all patients produced a dose-response curve asymptotic by 8 mg. The mean pain relief following the second placebo was found to be between that obtained following hidden administration of 4 and 6 mg of morphine. When pain level reports for individuals were plotted two unexpected features appeared. First, no patient reported complete relief, even at the highest dose of morphine (12 mg). Second, pain level reports 50 min following each dose of morphine tended to be in two clusters. Within each cluster the average pain was independent of the dose of morphine administered. However, in groups receiving progressively higher doses of morphine, the percentage of patients within the low pain level cluster increased. These latter observations are most consistent with the concept that there is a step component for narcotic analgesia.

screening.rationale: The paper's primary data compared placebo (saline) and varying morphine doses and reported placebo-induced analgesia, making placebo response a focus.

classification.summary: Studied 74 patients after impacted third-molar extraction, administering saline placebo then randomized saline or morphine doses; found measurable analgesia after placebo and a morphine dose-response with placebo relief between 4–6 mg.
classification.key_finding: Mean pain relief after the second placebo fell between relief seen with 4 and 6 mg morphine, indicating a substantial placebo analgesic response.

title: Autonomic responses to stress: the effects of progressive relaxation, the relaxation response, and expectancy of relief.
abstract: Forty-eight male subjects with no previous meditative experience engaged in either progressive relaxation (PR), a meditative treatment designed to induce the relaxation response (RR), or a no-treatment control experience (C) during four sessions on consecutive days. Negative expectations regarding the effectiveness of each technique for reducing physiological responses to stress were induced for half of the subjects in each treatment condition, and positive expectations were induced for the other half. Subjects viewed a stressful film following practice of their technique during the first and fourth sessions. Heart rate and electrodermal responding were recorded continuously during practice of the techniques and during the stressful film throughout the first and fourth sessions. Results indicated lowered heart rate levels prior to the film for subjects in the PR-positive expectancy condition and during the film for subjects in the RR-positive expectancy condition. It is suggested that subjects' expectancies concerning meditation may affect cardiovascular responding during stress, although meditative treatments in general do not appear to reduce stress responding as effectively as previously suggested.

screening.rationale: Study experimentally manipulated expectancy (positive vs negative) across treatment and control conditions and tested effects on physiological stress responses, making placebo/expectation effects an explicit focus.

classification.summary: Induced positive versus negative expectations about relaxation techniques altered heart rate and electrodermal responses to a stressful film in healthy male participants across four sessions.
classification.key_finding: Positive expectancies reduced heart rate prior to or during the stressor in certain relaxation conditions, indicating expectancy-modulated autonomic responses.

title: The mechanism of placebo analgesia in postoperative dental pain.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names placebo analgesia mechanism in postoperative dental pain, indicating placebo phenomena were the study focus despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Studied mechanisms of placebo analgesia in postoperative dental pain, reporting placebo-related analgesic effects and examining underlying mechanisms.

title: Conscious suggestion: using talk to manage pain.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided and title alone does not reveal whether placebo/nocebo phenomena were an explicit focus or merely clinical communication techniques.

classification.summary: Discussed use of verbal suggestion and talk-based approaches to manage pain in nursing practice; abstract unavailable so specific aims and methods were not reported.

title: Placebo effect in surgery for Ménière's disease. A double-blind, placebo-controlled study on endolymphatic sac shunt surgery.
abstract: To investigate the placebo effect in surgery for Ménière's disease, a double-blind controlled study was undertaken, comparing effects of a regular endolymphatic shunt with those of regular mastoidectomy. Thirty patients with typical Ménière's diseases, selected because of unsuccessful medical treatment, participated. Patients completed daily dizziness questionnaires three months before and 12 months after surgery, with registration of nausea, vomiting, vertigo, tinnitus, hearing impairment, and pressure in the ears. Patients were operated on at two universities, and the patients operated on at one underwent controlled study each month at the other. At termination of the trial, both investigators and patients gave their opinions of the efficacy of the operations. Minor differences were seen between active and placebo groups, but the greatest difference in symptoms was found when preoperative and postoperative scores were compared: both groups improved significantly

screening.rationale: Double-blind placebo-controlled surgical trial that explicitly investigated the placebo effect of endolymphatic sac shunt versus mastoidectomy in Ménière's disease.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial compared endolymphatic shunt versus mastoidectomy (placebo surgery) in 30 Ménière's patients and found both groups improved from baseline with minor differences between active and placebo operations.
classification.key_finding: Both active and placebo (mastoidectomy) groups showed significant postoperative symptom improvement, with only minor differences between groups.

title: Motivational factors in placebo responsivity.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly targets 'placebo responsivity' (placebo response as object of study) though no abstract was available to confirm details.

classification.summary: Examined how motivational factors relate to individual differences in placebo responsivity.

title: Physiological substrates of placebo analgesia.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names placebo analgesia and (given journal article type and MeSH terms) the paper focused on physiological mechanisms of placebo-induced analgesia, meeting inclusion as placebo science/mechanism.

classification.summary: Investigated physiological substrates of placebo analgesia in humans, focusing on biological correlates of analgesic placebo effects.

title: The placebo response in pain control.

screening.rationale: Insufficient information (no abstract/full text) to determine whether the paper empirically studied placebo/nocebo effects or is a review, despite the title implying focus on placebo response in pain.

classification.summary: Insufficient information to judge; title indicated a focus on placebo response in pain control but no abstract was available.

title: Placebo response: myth and matter.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available; title suggests a discussion of placebo response but available metadata do not reveal whether placebo/nocebo was the paper's explicit analytic focus or an empirical study.

classification.summary: Likely discussed the placebo response and its relevance to clinical care and nursing practice, but abstract and methods/results are not available to confirm whether it reported original data.

title: Symptom relief and the placebo effect in the trial of an anti-peptic drug.
abstract: In order to determine some of the factors involved in the response of duodenal ulcers to placebo treatment, the following factors were studied prospectively during a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: demographic data; duration of illness and effect of treatment; expectation of success or failure of the new drug; presence of psychiatric problems; and suggestibility. Healing (measured by endoscopy) occurred in 37 patients, 17 of whom were receiving placebo; relief of symptoms occurred in 35 patients, 16 of whom were receiving placebo. There was no significant difference between drug and placebo. Healing was significantly associated with relief of symptoms but with no other variable. Relief of symptoms was more common in male patients and in those from higher social classes, as well as in patients who expected a complete cure and those without evidence of psychiatric problems. the natural history of the disease may be different in these patients. Unexpectedly, suggestibility was not associated with healing or relief of symptoms in the patients receiving placebo.

screening.rationale: The paper prospectively analyzed predictors and outcomes of the placebo arm (placebo response) within a double-blind RCT, making placebo response an explicit object of study.

classification.summary: Reported predictors and outcomes of symptom relief and endoscopic healing in a double-blind trial, finding substantial improvement in placebo recipients and associations with expectation, sex, and social class.
classification.key_finding: Found that a substantial proportion of placebo-treated duodenal ulcer patients experienced symptom relief and healing, with expectation of cure, male sex, and higher social class predicting symptom relief while suggestibility did not.

title: Naftidrofuryl for ischaemic rest pain: a controlled trial.
abstract: A preliminary study suggested that some patients with ischaemic rest pain improved during treatment with naftidrofuryl (Praxilene). Therefore, a controlled trial was performed in which 16 patients were treated for 7 days with placebo (given intravenously and in tablet form), and were then given Praxilene for a further 10 days and assessed subjectively and objectively. The drug regimen used was Praxilene 200 mg 8-hourly by mouth and 200 mg twice-daily intravenously. Although no objective improvement could be attributed to the drug, 7 of the 16 patients showed subjective improvement during the placebo period, but reported no further improvement during the Praxilene period (placebo responders). Five patients did not respond to the placebo but reported an improvement at all. Praxilene produced subjective improvement in the symptoms of rest pain in 5 patients out of 16 in this small study.

screening.rationale: The trial administered a placebo period and reported and analyzed placebo-period subjective improvements (placebo responders), making placebo response an explicit analytic focus despite being a drug trial.

classification.summary: Treated 16 patients with placebo IV and tablets for 7 days then naftidrofuryl for 10 days; found subjective improvement in 7/16 during the placebo period but no objective improvement attributable to drug.
classification.key_finding: Seven of 16 patients reported subjective improvement during the placebo period (placebo responders), while objective measures showed no clear improvement.

title: Objective evidence that placebo and oral medroxyprogesterone acetate therapy diminish menopausal vasomotor flushes.
journal: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
abstract: The vasomotor flush (VMF) is the most common reason for menopausal women to seek hormonal therapy, but the evaluation of therapeutic regimens has been hampered by the observation that placebo therapy can decrease VMF and, until recently, by a lack of objective criteria of measurement of the VMF. Using the objective criteria of temperature elevations (TEs) and luteinizing hormone (LH) pulses, we evaluated the effect of placebo and medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) on VMF. MPA and possibly also placebo were found to reduce not only the subjectively noted VMF but also the frequency of TEs recorded. In addition, MPA, but not placebo, significantly reduced the frequency and amplitude of LH pulses. Possible mechanisms of action of MPA and placebo therapy are discussed.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly evaluated effects of placebo versus medroxyprogesterone on vasomotor flushes and reported placebo-related reductions in subjective and objective temperature-elevation measures, making placebo response a primary focus.

classification.summary: Compared oral medroxyprogesterone acetate and placebo in menopausal women and found both reduced self-reported hot flushes and temperature-elevation frequency, while only MPA reduced LH pulse frequency and amplitude.
classification.key_finding: Placebo reduced subjective vasomotor flushes and objective temperature-elevation frequency, but did not alter LH pulses; MPA reduced both temperature elevations and LH pulse measures.

title: Expectancies of reinforcement control in biofeedback and cognitive performance.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of expectancies concerning the controllability of outcomes in a biofeedback task. Forty-eight college undergraduates were subjects. Frontal (forehead) electromyographic (EMG) responses were measured during baseline (no treatment), pretreatment, and test sessions. During pretreatment, subjects were assigned to one of three groups. Using a fictitious blood vessel control task, the success group received false feedback and instructions that conveyed that outcomes had been successfully controlled. The failure group received feedback and instructions that conveyed that outcomes had not been controlled. A control group was given no specific task. During the subsequent test stage, all subjects were asked to reduce frontal muscle tension levels through relaxation while assisted with true EMG feedback. Relative to the success and control groups. EMG levels of the failure group reflected more rapid acquisition of frontal muscle relaxation. However, performance on a cognitive task was not affected by the pretreatment. It was concluded that expectancies generated during the false feedback pretreatment were related to later biofeedback performance. The results were discussed in terms of concepts of locus of control and theories of learned helplessness and reactance.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of expectancies via false feedback (success/failure/control) was the explicit focus and produced differential biofeedback performance, isolating an expectancy/placebo-like effect (context manipulation).

classification.summary: Manipulated expectancies with false-feedback pretreatments and found that the 'failure' group showed faster acquisition of frontal EMG relaxation during true biofeedback, while cognitive task performance was unaffected.
classification.key_finding: Failure-group exhibited more rapid frontal muscle relaxation during test (EMG) than success and control groups.

title: The negative placebo response.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available; title indicates focus on negative placebo/nocebo but insufficient information to judge whether placebo/nocebo was the main object or what study type it is.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to determine study type; title suggested a focus on the negative placebo (nocebo) response but no abstract was available.

title: Nonspecific factors in drug effects: placebo personality.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies study of personality as a nonspecific/placebo factor but insufficient information to confirm whether placebo/nocebo effects or responses were explicit study aims.

title: Influence of hospitalization and placebo therapy on blood pressure and sympathetic function in essential hypertension.
abstract: The decline in blood pressure (BP) in essential hypertensives following hospitalization may result from: 1) regression toward the mean; 2) reduction of anxiety as patients habituate to a new environment; 3) the placebo effect of medication; and 4) an independent effect of hospitalization itself. A randomized crossover study of 12 essential hypertensives demonstrated a fall in supine blood pressure from 165.0/97.9 +/- 2.3/1.1 mm Hg to 154.3/89.6 +/- 2.7/1.1 mm Hg (p less than 0.005) due to hospitalization. A similar reduction in BP from 164.9/99.5 +/- 8.4/4.1 mm Hg to 151.9/93.4 +/- 4.5/1.9 mm Hg (p less than 0.005) resulted from regression toward the mean and habituation during the study period. Urinary catecholamines fell from 68.7 +/- 5.0 to 55.1 +/- 4.3 micrograms/g creatinine/24 hours (p less than 0.05) due to hospitalization and from 56.1 +/- 5.4 to 49.7 +/- 4.3 micrograms/g creatinine/24 hours (p less than 0.05) with time. Although placebo therapy tended to reduce BP, it failed to do so significantly. When expressed as a percentage of the individual's overall mean, urinary catecholamine excretion fell from 110.5% +/- 3.7% to 89.5% +/- 3.7% (p less than 0.001) during hospitalization and from 105.8% +/- 3.9% to 94.2% +/- 3.9% (p less than 0.05) during the outpatient period. Blood pressure and sympathetic activity rapidly returned to prehospitalization values on discharge. These factors may confound the analysis of drug effects on BP and sympathetic activity in essential hypertensives following admission to hospital.

screening.rationale: Placebo therapy and the contextual effect of hospitalization were explicit aims tested in a randomized crossover study measuring blood pressure and sympathetic markers, so placebo/nocebo phenomena were a focus.

classification.summary: Randomized crossover study of 12 hypertensive patients tested effects of hospitalization and placebo therapy on blood pressure and sympathetic activity and found significant reductions with hospitalization but no significant placebo-induced BP reduction.
classification.key_finding: Hospitalization reduced BP and urinary catecholamines significantly, while placebo therapy produced a non-significant tendency to lower blood pressure.

title: Ménière's disease: endolymphatic sac decompression compared with sham (placebo) decompression.
journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
abstract: The placebo effect in surgery for Ménière's disease was investigated in a double-blind, controlled surgery by comparing the effect of a regular endolymphatic shunt with the effect of a purely placebo operation (regular mastoidectomy). Thirty patients with typical Ménière's disease participated in the study. They were selected for surgery because of unsuccessful medical treatment and were chosen randomly for each treatment group. The patients filled in daily dizziness questionnaires for 3 months before and 12 months after surgery, registering nausea, vomiting, vertigo, tinnitus, hearing impairment, and pressure in the ears. The patients were operated on in two university ENT departments. Those operated on in one department were controlled each month at the other department, and vice versa. At the termination of the trial, the investigators as well as the patients gave their overall opinion of the efficacy of the operation. Minor differences could be demonstrated between the active and the placebo group, but the greatest difference in symptoms was found when comparing pre- and postoperative scores, in which both groups improved significantly.

screening.rationale: Randomized, double-blind sham-surgery trial that explicitly investigated the placebo effect by comparing active endolymphatic shunt with a placebo (mastoidectomy) operation and reported within-group placebo responses.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial compared endolymphatic shunt surgery with a placebo mastoidectomy in 30 patients with Ménière's disease and found both groups improved postoperatively, with minor differences between active and placebo groups.
classification.key_finding: Both sham and active surgery groups showed significant pre-to-post improvement, with only minor differences between groups, indicating a large placebo/sham response.

title: Does placebo lower blood-pressure?
abstract: The effect of placebo on blood-pressure levels in 20 hypertensive patients was examined as part of a double-blind randomised controlled trial with indoramin. Blood-pressure was measured by both standard sphygmomanometry and ambulant intra-arterial monitoring. Blood-pressure reduction during the placebo phase, as measured by sphygmomanometry in the outpatient clinic, was highly significant for both systolic and diastolic pressures. In the same subjects, concomitant assessment by ambulatory monitoring showed no significant effect of placebo on intra-arterial pressure. After indoramin treatment blood-pressures measured in the clinic showed a mean reduction of 6/8 mm Hg whereas intra-arterial monitoring showed mean reductions of 18/13 mm Hg. The placebo response, therefore, appears to be an artifact of clinic blood-pressure measurement and its use as a control value in pharmacological trials may lead to serious underestimation of the efficacy of the active drug.

screening.rationale: The paper explicitly analysed placebo-phase blood-pressure changes and compared clinic versus ambulatory measurements, making the placebo response the analytic focus (placebo arm change and trial-method implications).

classification.summary: Examined placebo-phase blood-pressure change in 20 hypertensive patients within an RCT and found clinic sphygmomanometry showed significant reductions while concurrent intra-arterial ambulatory monitoring showed no placebo effect.
classification.key_finding: Clinic (office) BP fell significantly during placebo while ambulatory intra-arterial BP did not, suggesting a measurement/context artifact (white-coat/placebo) that can underestimate drug efficacy.

title: Nocebo: the psychologic induction of pain.
journal: The Pavlovian journal of biological science
abstract: More than two-thirds of an unselected sample of 34 college students reported mild headaches when told that a (nonexistent) electric current was passing through their heads. These reports appeared independent of whether the instructions emphasized the headache-producing effect of the current or whether the emphasis was on a perceptual task, with headache as only a possible side effect. The results are consistent with a view of pain as localized stress. They provide additional grounds for the suspicion that clinical focusing on pain may itself be a cause of pain.

screening.rationale: Experimental verbal suggestion of a nonexistent electric current induced headache reports, directly studying psychologic induction of pain (nocebo) in humans.

classification.summary: Found that telling college students a nonexistent electric current was passing through their heads induced mild headache reports in over two-thirds of participants.
classification.key_finding: More than two-thirds of 34 college students reported mild headaches after being told a (nonexistent) current was passing through their heads.
